narrative:

Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Even though many accepted students sit around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile, which the model saw as a clear warning sign for bar exam success. Your first-year ranking had a similar but smaller negative effect; you also finished in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged near the middle of their class.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 39, you scored above the average of 37.2 among accepted students, and this helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, the two weak class rankings outweighed the positive LSAT signal, tipping the final probability just above the acceptance threshold.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.4, middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were not major drivers of the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in the remaining law school years. Raising your ranking would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction. Consider reaching out to academic support services or a bar-prep tutor early. With targeted effort on class performance, you can shift the model’s outlook on a future application. (248 words)
